questions.stem: On a decision tree, what does a square represent?
options: A decision node, where the business chooses
A chance node, where the outcome is uncertain
The payoff at the end of a branch
The probability of an outcome
questions.why: Squares are decisions the business controls. Circles are chance nodes where the outcome depends on probability.
whyNot: That is a circle.
Payoffs are written at the ends of branches.
Probabilities are written on the branches.

questions.stem: Probabilities on branches from the same chance node must add up to:
options: the number of branches
the expected value
questions.why: They are expressed as decimals and must total 1, because one of the outcomes must happen.
whyNot: That would be correct if expressed as percentages, and the convention here is decimals summing to 1.
The number of branches is unrelated to the total.
The expected value is a money amount.

questions.stem: An option has a 0.6 chance of $90,000 and a 0.4 chance of $20,000. What is its expected value?
whyNot: This adds the two payoffs without weighting them.
That is the expected value of a different set of payoffs.
This appears to weight the payoffs the wrong way round.

questions.stem: An option has an expected value of $62,000 and costs $30,000. What is its net expected value?
questions.why: 62,000 - 30,000 = $32,000. Deducting the cost of the option before comparing is the step most candidates forget.
whyNot: This adds the cost instead of subtracting it.
That is the expected value before the cost is deducted.
That is the cost of the option.

questions.stem: Option A has an expected value of $62,000 and costs $30,000. Option B has $55,000 and costs $10,000. Which should be chosen?
options: B, because its net expected value of $45,000 exceeds A's $32,000
A, because its expected value is higher
A, because it costs more and so must be better
Neither, because both have positive expected values
questions.why: A has the higher expected value; B has the higher NET expected value. That reversal is exactly what these questions test.
whyNot: Expected value before cost is not the basis for the decision.
Cost is a reason against, not for.
Positive values mean both are viable; the question is which is better.

questions.stem: In which order should a decision tree be calculated?
options: Right to left, calculating expected values at each chance node
Left to right, starting from the decision
Top to bottom
The order does not matter
questions.why: You need the expected value of each outcome before you can compare the options that lead to them, so the calculation works backwards from the payoffs.
whyNot: You cannot evaluate the decision before the outcomes it leads to.
Not a meaningful direction for a tree.
Working forwards produces the wrong answer.

questions.stem: Why should a small business with no cash reserves look at the worst case as well as the expected value?
options: An expected value is an average that may never occur, and one bad outcome could be fatal
Expected values are always wrong
Small businesses cannot calculate probabilities
The worst case is always the most likely
questions.why: An expected value of $62,000 when outcomes are $90,000 or $20,000 describes neither. A business that cannot survive the $20,000 outcome should not treat the average as the decision.
whyNot: They are estimates, not necessarily wrong.
They can use the same estimates as anyone else.
It is one possible outcome, not the most likely.

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of a decision tree?
options: The probabilities are estimates, and changing them can reverse the decision
It cannot show more than two options
It ignores the cost of each option
It cannot be drawn by hand
questions.why: Both the probabilities and the payoffs are forecasts, so there are two layers of estimation. Shifting 0.6 to 0.5 can change which option wins.
whyNot: It can show any number of options.
Costs are written on the option branches and should be deducted.
It is normally drawn by hand.

questions.stem: Which factor does a decision tree ignore entirely?
options: Staff morale, reputation and strategic fit
The probability of each outcome
The payoff of each outcome
The cost of each option
questions.why: The model is purely financial. Qualitative factors may be decisive and appear nowhere in the calculation, which is why the tree informs the decision rather than making it.
whyNot: Probabilities are central to it.
Payoffs are central to it.
Costs appear on the option branches.
